# Pooja Singhal — Product Designer

> Product designer working across UX and UI. Former mathematics teacher.
> Available for full-time product design roles and a small number of contract
> projects. Contact: pooja.guptavv@gmail.com

Pooja Singhal designs digital products end to end — problem framing, user
research, information architecture, interaction design, interface design and
usability testing. She taught mathematics before moving into product design,
and brings that training to bear on design problems: break down uncertainty,
identify relationships, reason through the problem systematically before
proposing a solution.

Her stated approach to a project: understand the business and its goals;
research and analyse the problem space; prototype with AI; then design,
validate and refine — repeating as the work demands. The framework flexes per
project rather than being applied rigidly.

## Case study: MathzAI

An AI maths tutoring web app for students from roughly class 8 through
undergraduate. Pooja was the sole designer on a team of four (founder,
frontend, backend, and herself).

The core tension: the product's value is learning, but what a student at 11pm
actually wants is to finish their homework. Most AI tools spoon-feed results,
and a student handed a direct answer learns where the answer came from, not
where their own reasoning broke down. Her framing: an AI tutor should be as
deliberate about what it refuses to show as about what it shows.

The work covered competitive analysis (benchmarking how quickly rival tools
disclose a solution), moderated user testing, and a design system. Testing
surfaced three concrete failures: the three main features read as identical to
students; "Solution" and "Final Answer" were understood as one thing; and the
"Continue" button was stranded with no context. The redesign replaced passive
reading with step-by-step choices, named what the student got right in specific
terms rather than generic praise, and located the student with colour,
breadcrumbs and a step counter working at three different levels.

Visual direction had to be interesting without being childish — a fifteen-year-
old disengages from anything built for a ten-year-old — and trustworthy enough
that corrections are believed. Red and green were unavailable to the brand
palette, both already meaning wrong and right in correctness feedback. Roca for
headings, Avenir Next for body.

## Case study: Lister

A web app for discovering, creating and sharing lists on any topic, with
private and public lists and a distinction between people who can edit and
people who can only view.

Pooja designed low-fidelity wireframes, then used Claude Code to turn them into
functional prototypes for testing. She ran moderated usability sessions with
five participants — a mix of people she knew and recruited strangers — covering
searching for lists, duplicating, editing, and understanding ownership.

The design work resolved into four threads: unifying the workflow, simplifying
discovery, ensuring clarity and trust around who can do what, and making the
product responsive by design — rethinking the layout from the smallest screens
upward so content was prioritised and exposed rather than merely reflowed.

Success was framed around task completion, feature discovery and habit
formation.
